paras: The lynching of Tom Robinson and Bill Cephas took place at Bastrop, in Morehouse Parish, Louisiana, in early December 1882, when a body of men broke open the jail and hanged the two Black prisoners from a tree near the town. The two men were being held on a charge of shooting a young white man named Curry, who survived. The wire account, which said local opinion sided with the lynchers and blamed 'indulgent juries', ran in papers from Maine to California.

According to a special from Bastrop to the New Orleans Times-Democrat, Robinson and Cephas had been placed in the parish prison two days before the lynching, charged with shooting W. B. Curry. A Monroe dispatch placed the shooting in Gum Swamp, Morehouse parish, and the Weekly Clarion of Mississippi said the two had tried to kill Curry 'for his money'. A brief note in the Lake Charles Echo gave a different version, in which W. P. Curry, a clerk at Casonville, was 'assassinated' on the 6th by Tom Roberson, 'a drunken negro' whom Curry had whipped that day, and who escaped.

The same dispatches reported a second case nearby: a Black man named Wesley Andrews was accused of trying to kill a white man named McDowell outside Bastrop the previous Saturday and had been captured. A Louisiana state summary described McDowell as beaten senseless and robbed, with ax wounds to the head, and said Andrews had been arrested on the supposition that he did it.

At night, 'a determined body of indignant men' broke down the jail doors and took Robinson and Cephas out. The Donaldsonville Chief described the attackers as 'a body of masked men' and said the prisoners were hanged from a tree half a mile from town. The Bastrop correspondent wrote that the town learned of it the next morning, when the two were found hanging from the limb of a tree near Bastrop. Curry was then reported alive but in a dangerous condition, and the correspondent wrote that if he recovered his face would be disfigured for life.

The Bastrop special stated that public opinion was 'in sympathy with the lynchers' and that 'no desire to find them out is manifested.' No report of arrests, an inquest or a grand jury inquiry into the lynching appears in the coverage. Wesley Andrews's fate remained uncertain: the dispatches said only that 'Judge Lynch' was reported to have settled his case, while the Donaldsonville Chief two weeks later mentioned only his arrest.

The story went out by telegraph on December 8 in two forms, a short Monroe dispatch and a longer Bastrop or New Orleans dispatch, and appeared the next day in dailies in Portland, Augusta, Alexandria, Savannah, St. Paul and Sacramento. Headlines ranged from the plain 'LYNCHED.' and 'Lynching in Louisiana' to 'Sentenced by Judge Lynch' in the Portland Daily Press and 'Lawlessness in the South' in the Kennebec Journal. The Savannah Morning News headed the item 'A Community Resolved to Protect Itself' and ended it with the line that indulgent juries had 'aroused the people, who are determined that outrageous crimes shall not go unpunished.'

Weeklies from Montana to South Carolina reprinted the wire through mid-December, its details shifting as it went: Cephas became 'Casas' and 'Coppas', and the McDowell attack moved from three miles to eight or thirty. A 'Southern Gleanings' column printed in Alabama and Mississippi listed Wesley Andrews among those 'taken out and hanged', and a year-end chronology counted 'Three negroes lynched at Bastrop'. Within Louisiana, the Lake Charles Commercial reprinted the full Times-Democrat special under the headline 'Negroes Lynched in Morehouse Parish', while the Donaldsonville Chief wrote that Morehouse 'has been disgraced by a lynching affair'. No Black-press coverage of the case was found.

The date is uncertain: the abridged wire said the jail was broken on 'Wednesday night', December 6, but the Bastrop and Monroe dispatches of December 8 said 'last night', an Illinois digest gave 'the 7th', and the Donaldsonville Chief said 'Friday night of last week'. The Bastrop special, the most detailed local account, has the men jailed two days before and found hanging on the morning of December 8, which fits the night of December 7.

accounts.label: Bastrop special to the Times-Democrat
accounts.gist: Two colored men held two days for shooting Curry were taken from the broken jail 'last night' and found hanging from a tree near Bastrop in the morning; public opinion sided with the lynchers and no one sought them.

accounts.label: Monroe wire
accounts.gist: Tom Robinson, who shot young Curry in Gum Swamp, and another negro implicated with him were taken from the Bastrop jail by a mob 'last night' and hanged; Curry still alive.

accounts.label: Abridged Bastrop/New Orleans wire
accounts.gist: On 'Wednesday night' the jail doors were broken down and Robinson and Cephas hanged; Wesley Andrews was reported lynched for an attack on McDowell.

accounts.label: Louisiana state gleanings (Lake Charles Echo)
accounts.gist: Curry, a clerk at Casonville, was 'assassinated' on the 6th by Tom Roberson, a drunken negro Curry had whipped that day, who escaped; the item as printed says nothing of a lynching.

accounts.label: Louisiana state summary (Donaldsonville Chief)
accounts.gist: Masked men broke into the jail 'Friday night of last week', took Cephas and Robertson, charged with attempting to assassinate Curry, and hanged them half a mile from town.

framing.detail: The wire stated that public opinion sympathized with the lynchers and blamed 'indulgent juries'; the Savannah Morning News headed it 'A Community Resolved to Protect Itself'.
Northern and western dailies ran the short wire under neutral crime headlines such as 'LYNCHED.' and 'Lynching in Louisiana'.
The Kennebec Journal headed the Monroe wire 'Lawlessness in the South', and the Donaldsonville Chief wrote that Morehouse 'has been disgraced by a lynching affair'.

conflicts.note: The fuller Bastrop special says the men were jailed two days earlier after a shooting telegraphed on Wednesday, broken out 'last night' and found hanging 'this morning' (Dec. 8), which points to the night of Dec. 7; the abridged wire's 'Wednesday night' may conflate the shooting with the lynching.
The dispatches report Andrews only as 'reported' lynched, and the Donaldsonville Chief two weeks later says only that he was arrested.
